events.c: The first officer requested clearance for the flight to Beijing.
The crew requested permission to push back and start the engines. No distress was reported.
The tower cleared MH370 for takeoff.
MH370 departed Kuala Lumpur at about 16:42 UTC. The exact takeoff time isn't known.
Controllers cleared the aircraft to fly directly to IGARI and climb toward its assigned height.
Controllers cleared the aircraft to climb higher.
Controllers cleared the aircraft to climb to its cruising height.
The crew reported reaching cruising height; automatic data also showed the aircraft near that level.
The last automatic position message was sent, containing six earlier positions.
The crew again reported flying at cruising height. No problem was announced.
Controllers instructed MH370 to contact Ho Chi Minh control, but no contact with that center followed.
The captain acknowledged the handover in the last recorded radio reply.
The aircraft sent its last radar reply to Kota Bharu; its symbol remained on screens afterward.
The aircraft passed near IGARI.
The aircraft sent its last position broadcast. Missing height data do not show a plunge to ground level.
One of the aircraft's radar symbols disappeared from controllers' screens.
The aircraft's final position symbol disappeared from Kuala Lumpur radar. Military radar later tracked its turnback.
Radar detected the returning aircraft near Kota Bharu, but did not reliably establish its height.
Ho Chi Minh controllers asked Kuala Lumpur about the missing contact with MH370.
The first officer's phone registered near Penang. No call or message was recorded.
The airline repeatedly sent messages asking the crew to contact Ho Chi Minh. The aircraft never acknowledged them.
Military radar last detected the aircraft beyond MEKAR. No later exact position was recorded.
The aircraft reconnected to the satellite network, probably after a power interruption. The cause is unknown.
The aircraft's satellite equipment responded to an incoming call, but the call went unanswered.
The aircraft answered a satellite check. The data narrowed its possible location to a curve.
Another satellite reply narrowed the aircraft's possible location to a curve, without identifying an exact position.
Kuala Lumpur activated its rescue coordination center after a prolonged loss of contact.
The aircraft answered another satellite check, narrowing its possible location without giving an exact position.
Kuala Lumpur declared a distress phase. The declaration came from controllers, rather than the aircraft.
Another satellite reply narrowed the aircraft's possible location to a curve, without identifying an exact position.
A second satellite call went unanswered, although the aircraft's equipment responded.
The aircraft responded to a sixth satellite check, providing further satellite timing and frequency data.
The aircraft's satellite equipment requested another connection to the network.
The final aircraft transmission suggested a rapid descent, but did not establish when or where impact occurred.
A later satellite check received no reply from the aircraft.
Satellite analysis indicated the flight ended in the southern Indian Ocean, but did not establish an exact location.
The aerial search ended without confirmed MH370 debris. The search shifted toward the seabed.
A moving part of the right wing was found on Réunion and later confirmed to be from MH370.
A piece of the left wing was found in Mauritius and later confirmed to be from MH370.
A right wing section found on Pemba Island was linked to MH370 through its identifying numbers.
A review recommended searching about 25,000 additional square kilometers, north of much of the earlier search.
The government search stopped after covering more than 120,000 square kilometers without finding the main wreckage.
A review of the search left the cause of the disappearance unknown.
Ocean Infinity began searching the seabed and later expanded its search area.
Ocean Infinity ended its search without finding the aircraft, after surveying more than 112,000 square kilometers.
Investigators found the turnback likely involved manual control. Who controlled the aircraft and why remain unknown.
A proposed final location based on radio signals remained disputed by specialists.
Australian investigators continued encouraging more frequent aircraft tracking and equipment that automatically tracks aircraft in distress.
A study proposed a controlled eastward descent, but provided no new confirmed wreckage location.
Malaysia approved a renewed Ocean Infinity search in principle. A signed contract followed later.
Malaysia signed a search agreement covering about 15,000 square kilometers. Some surveying had already taken place.
The first search phase under the contract ended after running from March 25 to 28, 2025.
The second search phase under the contract began on December 31, 2025.
Ocean Infinity left the search area without confirmed wreckage findings, after both phases covered about 7,571 square kilometers.
Malaysia and Ocean Infinity told families that MH370's location remained unconfirmed.
Malaysia extended the search agreement through June 30, 2027. A restart date was not confirmed.
Radar records distinguish the aircraft's last replies from symbols that remained on screens afterward.

one_line: MH370 disappeared after leaving its route; its final location in the southern Indian Ocean remains unknown.
status_why: Radar, satellite data, and confirmed debris provide clues, but the main wreckage and cause remain unknown.
